title: How To Stop Excessive Talking
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin dismantles common teacher justifications for excessive classroom talking, such as calling students 'social butterflies' with chatting as their 'learning style.' He argues that framing talking as an inherent trait rather than a behavior removes the teacher's power to change it, and that whatever misbehavior a teacher excuses, they effectively accept. The article lays out a five-step solution: define when talking isn't allowed, explain why, model what silence looks like, show consequences via the classroom management plan, and enforce consistently. He stresses that a teacher's inner conviction that their approach is right and non-negotiable is what actually powers the whole system, since students can sense authenticity or its absence. The piece concludes that excessive talking isn't a fixed personality trait but a pattern the teacher has permitted through inconsistent responses.
points: Explaining away excessive talking as a personality trait or 'learning style' removes the teacher's power to actually change the behavior.
Whatever misbehavior a teacher justifies or excuses, they effectively accept and perpetuate.
A five-step process is recommended: define when talking isn't allowed, explain why, model silence, show consequences via the CM plan, and enforce.
A teacher's genuine, non-negotiable conviction in their approach is what students actually respond to, more than the specific words used.
Excessive talking is not an inherent student trait but a pattern shaped and permitted by the teacher's own consistency or lack of it.
quotes: You see, whatever misbehavior you justify, you accept. If you view talking instead of listening or focusing on work as just who your students are, then it will never stop.
Here at SCM, we believe that the entire premise that students are just the way they are, no matter the behavior, is hogwash. You decide how our students behave, not the other way around.
But like every area of classroom management, eliminating unwanted talking is simply a function of knowledge. It’s a matter of knowing what to do and then doing it.
When you know your approach is right and best for them, and you know you won’t accept anything less, then your students will know it too. They’ll hear it in your voice and see it on your face.

Talking when your students are supposed to be listening or working independently is not “just who they are.” It’s not a learning style or a personality trait. It’s not a cutesy social quirk or an acceptable excuse.
